newsitem.title: SPAIN: Latam must beware of complacency on reforms - experts.
newsitem.headline: Latam must beware of complacency on reforms - experts.

text.p: Latin America, revelling in soaring investment flows as economic reforms take hold, faces a better future than it has in decades, but experts said it must not slip into complacency.
Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) President Enrique Iglesias said that Latin America faced a dynamic future but rising capital flows should must not tempt the region to drag its feet on reform.

"The euphoria sometimes generated by massive inflows of capital can make us forget that this short term capital cannot make up for domestic savings," he told the bank's annual meeting in Barcelona, which ended on Wednesday.
Iglesias highlighted reforms to the region's social security systems as key to protecting it from volatility.
Mexico, which had long relied on short-term inflows, plunged into recession in 1995 after a peso devaluation made investors panic and wreaked havoc across the world's emerging markets.
Latin America has been buoyed by Mexico's recovery and by renewed confidence of investors as it embarks on a programme of far-reaching economic reform.
Capital flows into the region shot up to $60 billion in 1996 from just over $40 billion the previous year.
In its annual report released at the meeting, the IADB predicted average economic growth of 4.5 percent for Latin America and the Caribbean in 1997 after 3.5 percent in 1996.
After decades of double and triple digit inflation, rates fell last year to their lowest level since 1977, averaging 11 percent after 13 percent in 1995.

Exports grew about 13 percent and real investment rose by about six, the report said. As nation after nation fleshed out the report with positive accounts of their recent economic performance, the bullishness of international bankers at the meeting was clear.
Their optimism was unshaken by a continuing hostage crisis in Peru, political instability in Ecuador, U.S. decertification of Colombia as an anti-drugs ally and the threat of the same for Mexico.
But a handful of experts also sounded a note of caution.

"Just as markets have been impressed by recent progress, further progress will receive richer rewards... (but) it also means that slippage will receive swift punishment," said David Lipton, assistant secretary to the U.S. Treasury.
"We do not need to look far back in history to know that those capital inflows should not be taken for granted.".
William Rhodes, vice-chairman of Citibank, said the region had staged a remarkable recovery since the Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s.
"Out of the ashes Latin America has risen like a phoenix," said Rhodes, who headed the major banking advisory committees during the crisis.

But he added that he was concerned that the high capital flows might lead to reckless lending and the possibility that rising unemployment levels and endemic poverty might generate a backlash against reform.
"If (these countries) can't show consistent growth over time the populations may start rejecting some of these reforms," he said.

Earlier Iglesias said Latin America needed to double its growth to about seven percent before it could make serious inroads into the poverty endemic in the region, while health and education needed to be made priorities.
But he said: "At one point we believed in Latin America that we could carry on with any volume of short-term debt ... Nowadays we know better."
